items.text: Targets loss to follow-up after a positive FIT, testing risk-stratified navigation rather than merely re-demonstrating that navigation is effective; distinguishes predicting non-adherence from predicting intervention benefit.

External validation on a historical cohort, recalibration if necessary, then randomization within low/medium adherence strata can yield locally generalizable average intervention effects and model transfer insights.

Cost, risk-stratum allocation, implementation by real clinical staff, and qualitative research together provide knowledge for sustainable deployment, without treating mechanistic breakthroughs as the threshold of value.

The high-adherence stratum is observational only, so the gain of navigation for that stratum cannot be directly inferred; weak discrimination and a large detectable interaction limit claims about optimal targeting configurations.

Clinical contacts in different arms and out-of-hospital colonoscopy records may affect measurement and contamination; with blinded audits and a 10% usual-care spot check already in place, one cannot say there is no control at all, nor arbitrarily specify the overall direction of bias.

Feasibility and generalizability depend on local resources, reachable patients, navigator hours, and endoscopy capacity; one-year costs are interpreted per completed colonoscopy, and precision for rare cancers and subgroup conclusions is limited.
